studies.title: Effects of Citrulline Supplementation on Exercise Performance in Humans: A Review of the Current Literature.
studies.abstract: Gonzalez, AM and Trexler, ET. Effects of citrulline supplementation on exercise performance in humans: A review of the current literature. J Strength Cond Res 34(5): 1480-1495, 2020-L-citrulline, a nonessential amino acid found primarily in watermelon, has recently garnered much attention for its potential to augment L-arginine bioavailability, nitric oxide production, and exercise performance. Over the past decade, L-citrulline has received considerable scientific attention examining potentially ergogenic properties for both aerobic and anaerobic exercise performance. Thus, the purpose of this article is to summarize the theoretical rationale behind L-citrulline supplementation and to comprehensively review the available scientific evidence assessing the potential ergogenic value of L-citrulline supplementation on vascular function and exercise performance in humans. In addition, research that has investigated the potential synergistic effects of L-citrulline with other dietary ingredients (e.g., arginine, antioxidants, nitrates, and branched-chain amino acids) is reviewed. Oral L-citrulline and citrulline malate supplementation have shown to increase plasma citrulline and arginine concentrations, along with total nitrate and nitrite concentrations. Although blood flow enhancement is a proposed mechanism for the ergogenic potential of L-citrulline, evidence supporting acute improvements in vasodilation and skeletal muscle tissue perfusion after supplementation is scarce and inconsistent. Nevertheless, several studies have reported that L-citrulline supplementation can enhance exercise performance and recovery. Given the positive effects observed from some investigations, future studies should continue to investigate the effects of both acute and chronic supplementation with L-citrulline and citrulline malate on markers of blood flow and exercise performance and should seek to elucidate the mechanism underlying such effects.

studies.title: Effects of Acute Citrulline Malate Supplementation on Repeated 100 m Sprint Performance in Trained Sprinters: A Randomized Crossover Study.
studies.abstract: Strategies that support repeated high-intensity sprint performance are of considerable interest in competitive sprinting and team sports; however, evidence regarding acute citrulline malate (CM) supplementation during recovery intervals remains limited. This study examined the effects of acute CM supplementation on repeated 100 m sprint performance and rating of perceived exertion (RPE) in trained sprinters. Eleven trained male collegiate sprinters (100 m personal best: 11.22 ± 0.47 s; range: 10.35-12.16 s) completed randomized, double-blind, crossover trials (CM vs. placebo) on separate days. Each trial consisted of two maximal 100 m sprints separated by an 80-90 min recovery interval, during which 8 g of CM or placebo was ingested. Sprint performance was primarily evaluated using wind-adjusted 100 m sprint time based on Mureika's model. A significant condition × trial interaction was observed for wind-adjusted sprint time (p = 0.010), with a greater improvement in the CM condition (p = 0.008). RPE (Borg 6-20 scale) before the second sprint was lower (p = 0.004) following CM supplementation. These findings suggest that acute CM supplementation may modestly support repeated sprint performance under extended recovery conditions; however, the results should be interpreted with caution.

studies.title: Acute effect of citrulline malate on flow-mediated dilation and serum pharmacodynamics in healthy young males.
studies.abstract:
Introduction

The use of ergogenic compounds has gained increasing popularity among individuals who wish to improve performance and recover faster from their workouts. Among these products is citrulline malate (CitMal), a popular dietary supplement that is suggested to enhance nitric oxide (NO)-mediated vasodilation and muscle blood flow.

Methods

To evaluate effects on arterial function, flow-mediated dilation (FMD) of the brachial artery during active hyperemia was measured in 12 healthy, recreationally active males (23 ± 3 years) before and after (60- and 120-min post) consuming either 6 g CitMal, 12 g CitMal, or a taste-matched placebo. The study used a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, within-subject counterbalanced crossover design with ≥7-day washouts.

Results

Repeated measures ANOVA revealed no significant interaction (p = 0.315) or time effect (p = 0.649) in corrected FMD% at 60- and 120-min after intake of placebo, 6 g CitMal, and 12 g CitMal. There were also no significant differences (p = 0.301) between doses at any timepoint. A subgroup of six participants completed two additional visits to assess the effect of CitMal ingestion on serum markers involved in NO production. Over 120-min post-consumption, both doses significantly increased peak serum concentrations of citrulline (6 g: 504.7 ± 139.7; 12 g: 881.9 ± 216.7 μM), arginine (6 g: 70.2 ± 20.4; 12 g: 101.8 ± 36.2 μM), and ornithine (6 g: 27.9 ± 14.2; 12 g: 56.5 ± 30.0 μM) from baseline (all p < 0.001), with greater increases following 12 g (all p < 0.05). Likewise, arginine-to-dimethylarginine ratios (SDMA and ADMA) increased from baseline (SDMA, 6 g: 114.1 ± 24.2; 12 g: 166.2 ± 43.7; ADMA, 6 g: 119.2 ± 31.8; 12 g: 169.1 ± 29.1; all p < 0.001), with greater increases following 12 g (p < 0.05).

Discussion

Collectively, these findings suggest that neither 6 g nor 12 g of CitMal significantly enhance FMD within 120 min, despite marked increases in biochemical markers favorable to NO production. To our knowledge, this is the first study to compare acute doses of CitMal up to 12 g in relation to brachial artery FMD. These results indicate that acute vascular responses to CitMal may be limited by physiological ceiling effects and that potential vascular benefits may depend on longer-term supplementation, the presence of an exercise stimulus, or populations with impaired endothelial function.

The Effect of a Single Dose of Citrulline on the Physical Performance of Soccer-Specific Exercise in Adult Elite Soccer Players (A Pilot Randomized Double-Blind
studies.abstract: The purpose of this study was to evaluate the effect of a single intake of citrulline at 3 g and 6 g doses in adult elite soccer players performing sport-specific exercise. This randomized double-blind placebo-controlled study analyzed 18 soccer players from the top divisions of three European countries. Participants were randomized into three groups of six each and performed a field-based soccer-specific test for 18 min. Comparative analysis of heart rate, fatigue and post-exercise recovery was conducted. There were no statistically significant differences in most of the analyzed parameters, nor at any of the time points for lactate concentration. Players' RPE exercise test score did not reveal any differences. Neither a single intake of 3 g nor of 6 g of citrulline malate affected physical performance, subjective feelings of fatigue or post-exercise recovery in adult elite soccer players who performed a soccer-specific test.

studies.title: The Effect of Citrulline Malate Supplementation on Muscle Fatigue Among Healthy Participants.
studies.abstract: Farney, TM, Bliss, MV, Hearon, CM, and Salazar, DA. The effect of citrulline malate supplementation on muscle fatigue among healthy participants. J Strength Cond Res 33(9): 2464-2470, 2019-The focus of the investigation was to examine the effects of citrulline malate (CM) on muscular fatigue in healthy, recreationally trained participants. Twelve participants (men = 6 and women = 6) (24.1 ± 3.9 years) visited the laboratory on 3 separate days, all separated by 1 week. Each visit consisted of consuming 1 of 3 treatments: placebo, CM (8 g), and control in which no drink mixture was consumed. For each day of testing, participants consumed assigned treatment and performed 1 high-intensity exercise trial consisting of squats, lunge jumps, squat jumps, and lateral jumps. Participants performed the exercises in the listed order, which was designated as 1 round. Each participant performed 3 rounds, with the work-to-rest ratio being 20 seconds of work and 30 seconds of rest. A 1-minute rest was given between rounds. A pre/post-exercise isokinetic leg extension test was performed to measure for peak power, peak torque, and rate of fatigue. In addition, blood lactate was obtained pre/post-exercise. There were no treatment or interaction effects (p > 0.05) for peak torque, peak power, rate of fatigue, or blood lactate accumulation. However, there was a statistical significant decrease from pre/post-exercise for peak torque (p = 0.003), peak power (p = 0.003), and rate of fatigue (p = 0.001). In addition, lactate accumulation did increase significantly from pre/post-exercise (p = 0.0001). Finally, neither total work nor final heart rate was statistically significant between the treatments (p > 0.05). Citrulline malate was not effective in improving performance or alleviating fatigue after a high-intensity exercise session.

studies.title: Eight weeks of resistance training in conjunction with glutathione and L-Citrulline supplementation increases lean mass and has no adverse effects on blood clin
studies.abstract: Supplementation of combined glutathione (GSH) with L-citrulline in response to a single bout of resistance exercise has been shown to increase plasma nitric oxide metabolites, nitrite and nitrate and cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP), which may play a role in muscle protein synthesis. As a result, in response to resistance training (RT) these responses may establish a role for GSH + L-citrulline to increase muscle mass. This study attempted to determine the effects of an 8-week RT program in conjunction with GSH (Setria®) + L-citrulline, L-citrulline-malate, or placebo supplementation on lean mass and its association with muscle strength. The secondary purpose was to assess the safety of such supplementation protocol by assessing clinical chemistry markers. In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled design, 75 resistance-trained males were randomly assigned to ingest GSH + L-citrulline (GSH + CIT), L-citrulline-malate, or cellulose placebo daily while also participating in 8 weeks of RT. The full dose of each supplement was delivered in capsules that were identical in weight, size, shape, and color. Participants completed testing sessions for body composition and muscle strength before and after 4 and 8 weeks of RT and supplementation. Venous blood samples were obtained before and after 8 weeks. Leg press was increased with RT but was not significantly different between groups (p > 0.05); however, bench press strength was not increased with RT (p > 0.05). There were no significant changes in total body mass, fat mass, or total body water during 8 weeks of RT and supplementation. Lean mass increased in both GSH + CIT when compared to PLC; however, the increase was significant only after 4 weeks. Lean mass and strength were positively correlated (p < 0.05) in GSH + CIT, but not CIT-malate or PLC. Neither RT nor supplementation had any significant effects on blood clinical chemistry variables (p > 0.05). Compared to PLC, supplementation of GSH + CIT during resistance training increased lean mass after 4 weeks of RT and was positively associated with muscle strength. However, after 8 weeks of RT there were no significant differences in any of the measured variables.

studies.title: Citrulline malate supplementation does not improve German Volume Training performance or reduce muscle soreness in moderately trained males and females.
studies.abstract: Use of supplements to aid performance is common practice amongst recreationally active individuals, including those without a sufficient evidence base. This investigation sought to assess whether acute supplementation with 8 g of citrulline malate (CM) (1.11: 1 ratio) would improve anaerobic performance. A randomised double blind placebo control trial was employed, using a counterbalanced design. We recruited recreationally active men and women to take part in an isokinetic chair protocol, based on German Volume Training (GVT) whereby participants attempted to perform 10 sets of 10 repetitions against a force representing 70% of their peak concentric force. The number of repetitions achieved over the course of the GVT was 94.0 ± 7.9 and 90.9 ± 13.9 for placebo and CM respectively. There was no significant difference between the placebo and CM treatment for number of repetitions (P = 0.33), isometric (P = 0.60), concentric (P = 0.38), or eccentric (P = 0.65) peak force following the GVT. Total muscle soreness was significantly higher in the CM compared to the placebo treatment following the GVT protocol over 72 h (P = 0.01); although this was not accompanied by a greater workload/number of repetitions in the CM group. We conclude that an acute dose of CM does not significantly affect anaerobic performance using an isokinetic chair in recreational active participants. Practical implications include precaution in recommending CM supplementation. Coaches and athletes should be aware of the disparity between the chemical analyses of the products reviewed in the present investigation versus the manufacturers' claims.

studies.title: Acute Effect of Citrulline Malate Supplementation on Upper-Body Resistance Exercise Performance in Recreationally Resistance-Trained Men.
studies.abstract: Gonzalez, AM, Spitz, RW, Ghigiarelli, JJ, Sell, KM, and Mangine, GT. Acute effect of citrulline malate supplementation on upper-body resistance exercise performance in recreationally resistance-trained men. J Strength Cond Res 32(11): 3088-3094, 2018-To investigate the effect of citrulline malate (CM) supplementation on upper-body resistance exercise performance, 12 recreationally resistance-trained men (21.4 ± 1.6 years; 163.0 ± 46.2 cm; 85.0 ± 12.4 kg) underwent 2 testing sessions administered in a randomized, double-blind fashion. During each visit, participants were provided either 8 g of CM or a placebo (PL) 40 minutes before beginning a standardized warm-up and initiating a barbell bench press resistance exercise protocol consisting of 5 sets of 15 repetitions at 75% 1 repetition maximum with 2-minute rest intervals. Participants were instructed to complete as many repetitions as possible until either reaching 15 repetitions or muscular failure. Total number of repetitions performed and power output were recorded for each set. Subjective measures of energy, focus, fatigue, and perceived exertion, along with muscle thickness of the triceps brachii, were assessed before and after exercise. Significant (p ≤ 0.05) main effects for time were observed for all variables except for subjective feelings of energy (p = 0.085). A group × time interaction (F = 2.86, p = 0.034, n = 0.21) was observed for repetitions performed, where participants performed more (p = 0.015) repetitions on set 3 during PL (5.7 ± 1.2 repetitions) compared with CM (4.6 ± 1.2 repetitions). However, during set 4, participants tended (p = 0.089) to perform more repetitions during CM (4.8 ± 1.8 repetitions) compared with PL (4.3 ± 1.3 repetitions). No other differences were observed between trials. Supplementation with 8 g of CM 40 minutes before the barbell bench press resistance exercise protocol did not increase exercise performance, augment the muscle swelling response to training, or alter subjective measures of focus, energy, and fatigue in recreationally resistance-trained men.

studies.title: Citrulline Malate Does Not Improve Muscle Recovery after Resistance Exercise in Untrained Young Adult Men.
studies.abstract: The effects of citrulline malate (CM) on muscle recovery from resistance exercise remains unknown. We aimed to determine if citrulline malate supplementation improves muscle recovery after a single session of high-intensity resistance exercise (RE) in untrained young adult men. Nine young adult men (24.0 ± 3.3 years) participated in a double-blind crossover study in which they received 6 g of CM and placebo (PL) on two occasions, separated by a seven-day washout period. Each occasion consisted of a single session of high-intensity RE (0 h) and three subsequent fatigue tests sessions (at 24, 48, and 72 h) to assess the time course of muscle recovery. During the tests sessions, we assessed the following variables: number of maximum repetitions, electromyographic signal (i.e., root mean square (RMS) and median frequency (MF)), muscle soreness and perceived exertion, as well as blood levels of creatine kinase (CK), lactate, insulin, and testosterone:cortisol ratio. CK levels increased at 24 h post-exercise and remained elevate at 48 and 72 h, with no difference between CM and PL conditions. Muscle soreness increased at 24 h post-exercise, which progressively returned to baseline at 72 h in both conditions. Lactate levels increased immediately post-exercise and remained elevated at 24, 48, and 72 h in both conditions. No significant treatment × time interaction was found for all dependents variables (maximum repetitions, perceived exertion, CK, lactate, RMS, MF, and testosterone:cortisol ratio) during the recovery period. In conclusion, our data indicate that CM supplementation (single 6 g dose pre-workout) does not improve the muscle recovery process following a high-intensity RE session in untrained young adult men.

studies.title: Acute Citrulline-Malate Supplementation and High-Intensity Cycling Performance.
studies.abstract: Cunniffe, B, Papageorgiou, M, O'Brien, B, Davies, NA, Grimble, GK, and Cardinale, M. Acute citrulline-malate supplementation and high-intensity cycling performance. J Strength Cond Res 30(9): 2638-2647, 2016-Dietary L-citrulline-malate (CM) consumption has been suggested to improve skeletal muscle metabolism and contractile efficiency, which would be expected to predispose exercising individuals to greater fatigue resistance. The purpose of this study was to examine the effects of CM supplementation on acid-base balance and high-intensity exercise performance. In a double-blind, placebo-controlled, crossover study, 10 well-trained males consumed either 12 g of CM (in 400 ml) or lemon sugar-free cordial (placebo [PL]) 60 minutes before completion of 2 exercise trials. Each trial consisted of subjects performing 10 (×15 seconds) maximal cycle sprints (with 30-second rest intervals) followed by 5 minutes recovery before completing a cycle time-to-exhaustion test (TTE) at 100% of individual peak power (PP). Significant increases in plasma concentrations of citrulline (8.8-fold), ornithine (3.9-fold), and glutamine (1.3-fold) were observed 60 minutes after supplementation in the CM trial only (p ≤ 0.05) and none of the subjects experienced gastrointestinal side-effects during testing. Significantly higher exercise heart rates were observed in CM condition (vs. PL) although no between trial differences in performance related variables (TTE: [120 ± 61 seconds CM vs. 113 ± 50 seconds PL]), PP or mean power, ([power fatigue index: 36 ± 16% CM vs. 28 ± 18% PL]), subjective rating of perceived exertion or measures of acid-base balance (pH, lactate, bicarbonate, base-excess) were observed (p > 0.05). This study demonstrated that acute supplementation of 12 g CM does not provide acute ergogenic benefits using the protocol implemented in this study in well-trained males.

studies.title: Citrulline malate enhances athletic anaerobic performance and relieves muscle soreness.
studies.abstract: The purpose of the present study was to determine the effects of a single dose of citrulline malate (CM) on the performance of flat barbell bench presses as an anaerobic exercise and in terms of decreasing muscle soreness after exercise. Forty-one men performed 2 consecutive pectoral training session protocols (16 sets). The study was performed as a randomized, double-blind, 2-period crossover design. Eight grams of CM was used in 1 of the 2 training sessions, and a placebo was used in the other. The subjects' resistance was tested using the repetitions to fatigue test, at 80% of their predetermined 1 repetition maximum (RM), in the 8 sets of flat barbell bench presses during the pectoral training session (S1-4 and S1'-4'). The p-value was 0.05. The number of repetitions showed a significant increase from placebo treatment to CM treatment from the third set evaluated (p <0.0001). This increase was positively correlated with the number of sets, achieving 52.92% more repetitions and the 100% of response in the last set (S4'). A significant decrease of 40% in muscle soreness at 24 hours and 48 hours after the pectoral training session and a higher percentage response than 90% was achieved with CM supplementation. The only side effect reported was a feeling of stomach discomfort in 14.63% of the subjects. We conclude that the use of CM might be useful to increase athletic performance in high-intensity anaerobic exercises with short rest times and to relieve postexercise muscle soreness. Thus, athletes undergoing intensive preparation involving a high level of training or in competitive events might profit from CM.

studies.title: L-citrulline-malate influence over branched chain amino acid utilization during exercise.
studies.abstract: Exhaustive exercise induces disturbances in metabolic homeostasis which can result in amino acid catabolism and limited L-arginine availability. Oral L-citrulline supplementation raises plasma L-arginine concentration and augments NO-dependent signalling. Our aim was to evaluate the effects of diet supplementation with L-citrulline-malate prior to intense exercise on the metabolic handle of plasma amino acids and on the products of metabolism of arginine as creatinine, urea and nitrite and the possible effects on the hormonal levels. Seventeen voluntary male pre-professional cyclists were randomly assigned to one of two groups: control or supplemented (6 g L-citrulline-malate 2 h prior exercise) and participated in a 137-km cycling stage. Blood samples were taken in basal conditions, 15 min after the race and 3 h post race (recovery). Most essential amino acids significantly decreased their plasma concentration as a result of exercise; however, most non-essential amino acids tended to significantly increase their concentration. Citrulline-malate ingestion significantly increased the plasma concentration of citrulline, arginine, ornithine, urea, creatinine and nitrite (p < 0.05) and significantly decreased the isoleucine concentration from basal measures to after exercise (p < 0.05). Insulin levels significantly increased after exercise in both groups (p < 0.05) returning to basal values at recovery. Growth hormone increased after exercise in both groups, although the increase was higher in the citrulline-malate supplemented group (p < 0.05). L-citrulline-malate supplementation can enhance the use of amino acids, especially the branched chain amino acids during exercise and also enhance the production of arginine-derived metabolites such as nitrite, creatinine, ornithine and urea.

studies.title: Effects of L-citrulline oral supplementation on polymorphonuclear neutrophils oxidative burst and nitric oxide production after exercise.
studies.abstract: Seventeen volunteer male professional cyclists were randomly assigned to control or supplemented (6 g L-citrulline-malate) groups and participated in a cycling stage. Blood samples were taken in basal conditions, after the race and 3 h post-race. Citrulline supplementation significantly increased plasma concentration of both arginine and citrulline after the stage only in the supplemented group. Polymorphonuclear neutrophils (PMNs) from controls responded to exercise with a progressive decrease in ROS production. Supplemented PMNs significantly increased ROS production after exercise compared to basal values and diminished to values lower than basal at recovery. PMN nitrite concentration was significantly higher after exercise and recovery only in the supplemented group. Markers of oxidative damage-CK, LDH, malondialdehyde-and DNA damage remained unchanged in both groups. In conclusion, oral L-citrulline administration previous to a cycling stage increases plasma arginine availability for NO synthesis and PMNs priming for oxidative burst without oxidative damage.

studies.title: Effect of citrulline malate supplementation on muscle function and bioenergetics during short-term repeated bouts of fatiguing exercise.
studies.abstract: Citrulline malate (CM) has been shown to improve muscle performance in healthy participants during a single exercise session. Yet, within the framework of exercises repeated at close time interval, the consequences of CM ingestion on mechanical performance are controversial and the bioenergetics side remains undocumented. The aim of this double-blind placebo-controlled study was to evaluate in vivo the effect of short-term (7 doses in 48 h) oral administration of CM upon gastrocnemius muscle function and bioenergetics using non-invasive multimodal NMR techniques in healthy rats. The experimental protocol consisted of two 6-min bouts of fatiguing exercise spaced by an 8-min recovery period. CM treatment did not affect the basal bioenergetics status and increased the half-fatigue time during the first exercise bout. With exercise repetition, it prevented PCr cost alteration and decreased both the glycolytic ATP production and the contractile ATP cost in working muscle, but these changes were not associated to any improvement in mechanical performance. In addition, CM did not influence the replenishment of high-energy phosphorylated compounds during the post-exercise recovery periods. Therefore, short-term CM administration enhances muscle bioenergetics throughout fatiguing bouts of exercise repeated at close time interval but this enhancement does not benefit to mechanical performance.

studies.title: Acute and Chronic Citrulline Malate Supplementation on Muscle Contractile Properties and Fatigue Rate of the Quadriceps.
studies.abstract: This study compared the acute and chronic impact of citrulline malate (CM) supplementation on muscle contractile properties and fatigue rate of the quadriceps. Eighteen recreationally trained males consumed both a placebo (PL) and CM treatment for two separate dosing periods. The first experimental testing session for each dosing period was considered the baseline day, the second session the acute day, and the third session the chronic day, which followed seven consecutive days of supplementation. All testing sessions included exercising on a cycle ergometer at 50%-60% of their max power output for 30 min followed by performing the Thorstensson test on an isokinetic dynamometer. A two-way (Supplement × Time) analysis of variance with repeated measures resulted in no significant interactions (p > .05) (PL: baseline day, acute day, chronic day vs. CM: baseline day, acute day, chronic day) for peak power (in watts) (469 ± 81, 490 ± 97, 502 ± 99 vs. 464 ± 85, 480 ± 103, 501 ± 81); peak torque (in newton meters) (150 ± 26, 157 ± 32, 161 ± 31 vs. 149 ± 27, 156 ± 33, 161 ± 26); fatigue rate (in percentage) (57 ± 9, 57 ± 10, 58 ± 9 vs. 57 ± 10, 56 ± 9, 58 ± 9); and heart rate (in beats per minute) (156 ± 17, 146 ± 13, 146 ± 9 vs. 155 ± 11, 146 ± 11, 146 ± 9). The results of this study suggest that neither acute nor chronic supplementation of CM had an effect on recovery or fatigue rate of the quadriceps.

studies.title: Citrulline/malate promotes aerobic energy production in human exercising muscle.
studies.abstract:
Background

Previous studies have shown an antiasthenic effect of citrulline/malate (CM) but the mechanism of action at the muscular level remains unknown.

Objective

To investigate the effects of CM supplementation on muscle energetics.

Methods

Eighteen men complaining of fatigue but with no documented disease were included in the study. A rest-exercise (finger flexions)-recovery protocol was performed twice before (D-7 and D0), three times during (D3, D8, D15), and once after (D22) 15 days of oral supplementation with 6 g/day CM. Metabolism of the flexor digitorum superficialis was analysed by (31)P magnetic resonance spectroscopy at 4.7 T.

Results

Metabolic variables measured twice before CM ingestion showed no differences, indicating good reproducibility of measurements and no learning effect from repeating the exercise protocol. CM ingestion resulted in a significant reduction in the sensation of fatigue, a 34% increase in the rate of oxidative ATP production during exercise, and a 20% increase in the rate of phosphocreatine recovery after exercise, indicating a larger contribution of oxidative ATP synthesis to energy production. Considering subjects individually and variables characterising aerobic function, extrema were measured after either eight or 15 days of treatment, indicating chronological heterogeneity of treatment induced changes. One way analysis of variance confirmed improved aerobic function, which may be the result of an enhanced malate supply activating ATP production from the tricarboxylic acid cycle through anaplerotic reactions.

Conclusion

The changes in muscle metabolism produced by CM treatment indicate that CM may promote aerobic energy production.

studies.title: Citrulline malate supplementation increases muscle efficiency in rat skeletal muscle.
studies.abstract: Citrulline malate (CM; CAS 54940-97-5, Stimol®) is known to limit the deleterious effect of asthenic state on muscle function, but its effect under healthy condition remains poorly documented. The aim of this longitudinal double-blind study was to investigate the effect of oral ingestion of CM on muscle mechanical performance and bioenergetics in normal rat. Gastrocnemius muscle function was investigated strictly non-invasively using nuclear magnetic resonance techniques. A standardized rest-stimulation- (5.7 min of repeated isometric contractions electrically induced by transcutaneous stimulation at a frequency of 3.3 Hz) recovery-protocol was performed twice, i.e., before (t(0)-24 h) and after (t(0)+48 h) CM (3 g/kg/day) or vehicle treatment. CM supplementation did not affect PCr/ATP ratio, [PCr], [Pi], [ATP] and intracellular pH at rest. During the stimulation period, it lead to a 23% enhancement of specific force production that was associated to significant decrease in both PCr (28%) and oxidative (32%) costs of contraction, but had no effect on the time-courses of phosphorylated compounds and intracellular pH. Furthermore, both the rate of PCr resynthesis during the post-stimulation period (VPCr(rec)) and the oxidative ATP synthesis capacity (Q(max)) remained unaffected by CM treatment. These data demonstrate that CM supplementation under healthy condition has an ergogenic effect associated to an improvement of muscular contraction efficiency.

studies.title: Beneficial effects of citrulline malate on skeletal muscle function in endotoxemic rat.
studies.abstract: Although citrulline malate (CM; CAS 54940-97-5, Stimol) is used against fatigue states, its anti-asthenic effect remains poorly documented. The objective of this double-blind study was to evaluate the effect of oral ingestion of CM on a rat model of asthenia, using in situ (31)Phosphorus magnetic resonance spectroscopy ((31)P-MRS). Muscle weakness was induced by intraperitoneal injections of Klebsiella pneumoniae endotoxin (lipopolysaccharides at 3 mg/kg) at t(0) and t(0)+24 h. For each animal, muscle function was investigated strictly non-invasively before (t(0)-24 h) and during (t(0)+48 h) endotoxemia, through a standardized rest-stimulation-recovery protocol. The transcutaneous electrical stimulation protocol consisted of 5.7 min of repeated isometric contractions at a frequency of 3.3 Hz, and force production was measured with an ergometer. CM supplementation in endotoxemic animals prevented the basal phosphocreatine/ATP ratio reduction and normalized the intracellular pH (pH(i)) time-course during muscular activity as a sign of an effect at the muscle energetics level. In addition, CM treatment avoided the endotoxemia-induced decline in developed force. These results demonstrate the efficiency of CM for limiting skeletal muscle dysfunction in rats treated with bacterial endotoxin.

studies.title: Effects of citrulline malate on bacterial lipopolysaccharide induced endotoxemia in rats.
studies.abstract: The administration of endotoxins to rats as lipopolysaccharides (LPS) induces a state of exhaustion, in which the main symptoms are febrile hyperthermia, reduced food intake, decreased body weight, and reduced muscle performance in treadmill tests. Underlying the physiological and behavioral disturbances due to the LPS is the activation of macrophages that release cytokines (interleukin-1, tumor necrosis factor a) and NO. The cellular responses are intended to maintain homeostasis. Provision of citrulline as citrulline malate (CAS 54940-97-5, Stimol), an antifatigue substance, improved muscle performance, but had no effect on the body temperature or on the body weight of these animals weakened by LPS. The presence of citrulline in the NO synthesis pathway, or its participation in the speeded up elimination of ammonia and lactates, the main products of muscle metabolism, might explain the effects of citrulline malate in rats treated with LPS.

studies.title: Overview of mechanisms related to citrulline malate supplementation and different methods of high-intensity interval training on sports performance: A narrative
studies.abstract: Regular exercise is a practical non-pharmacological approach to maintaining physical and mental health through rehabilitation and prevention of chronic diseases due to its cardiovascular, cardiorespiratory, neurological, and neuromuscular benefits. Despite awareness of the benefits of exercise, a “lack of time” has proven to be the most common impediment to regular activity. Thus, a time-efficient and potentially enjoyable training modality with growing popularity is high-intensity interval training (HIIT). HIIT incorporates intermittent bouts of work and recovery intervals performed at an intensity close to maximal oxygen consumption (VO₂max). HIIT is considered to have equivalent or superior benefits compared to moderate-intensity continuous training (MICT). This narrative review focuses on the mechanisms of Citrulline Malate (CM) supplementation and various modes of HIIT on exercise performance. CM serves as a nitric-oxide enhancer leading to improved aerobic and anaerobic exercise performance by increasing muscle adenosine triphosphate (ATP) production, vasodilation, and blood flow to the active musculature and boosting work capacity. This article reviews the mechanisms related to CM supplementation and different modes of HIIT on exercise performance. Even though a single, acute 8 g dose of CM has been recommended, its mechanism of action remains to be seen due to the synergistic impact of both components (citrulline and malate). Moreover, the limited evidence for the standard level of supplement use and source of purchase results in athletes’ self-prescription of supplements. Therefore, to reduce the risk of accidental doping or toxicity, further studies should continue to investigate the optimal dose, timing, mechanism of action, as well as reliable sources of purchase for CM consumption.

studies.title: Acute Effect of Citrulline Malate on Repetition Performance During Strength Training: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
studies.abstract: Citrulline malate (CitMal) is a dietary supplement that is suggested to enhance strength training performance. However, there is conflicting evidence on this matter. Thus, the purpose of this meta-analysis was to determine whether supplementing with CitMal prior to strength training could increase the total number of repetitions performed before reaching voluntary muscular failure. A systematic search was conducted wherein the inclusion criteria were double-blind, placebo-controlled studies in healthy participants that examined the effect of CitMal on repetitions to failure during upper body and lower body resistance exercises. The Hedges's g standardized mean differences (SMD) between the placebo and CitMal trials were calculated and used in a random effect model. Two separate subanalyses were performed for upper body and lower body exercises. Eight studies, including 137 participants who consisted of strength-trained men (n = 101) and women (n = 26) in addition to untrained men (n = 9), fulfilled the inclusion criteria. Across the studies, 14 single-joint and multijoint exercises were performed with an average of 51 ± 23 total repetitions during 5 ± 3 sets per exercise at ∼70% of one-repetition maximum. Supplementing with 6-8 g of CitMal 40-60 min before exercise increased repetitions by 3 ± 5 (6.4 ± 7.9%) compared with placebo (p = .022) with a small SMD (0.196). The subanalysis for the lower body resulted in a tendency for an effect of the supplement (8.1 ± 8.4%, SMD: 0.27, p = .051) with no significant effect for the upper body (5.7 ± 8.4%, SMD: 0.16, p = .131). The current analysis observed a small ergogenic effect of CitMal compared with placebo. Acute CitMal supplementation may, therefore, delay fatigue and enhance muscle endurance during high-intensity strength training.

studies.title: Effects of Citrulline Supplementation on Exercise Performance in Humans: A Review of the Current Literature.
studies.abstract: Gonzalez, AM and Trexler, ET. Effects of citrulline supplementation on exercise performance in humans: A review of the current literature. J Strength Cond Res 34(5): 1480-1495, 2020-L-citrulline, a nonessential amino acid found primarily in watermelon, has recently garnered much attention for its potential to augment L-arginine bioavailability, nitric oxide production, and exercise performance. Over the past decade, L-citrulline has received considerable scientific attention examining potentially ergogenic properties for both aerobic and anaerobic exercise performance. Thus, the purpose of this article is to summarize the theoretical rationale behind L-citrulline supplementation and to comprehensively review the available scientific evidence assessing the potential ergogenic value of L-citrulline supplementation on vascular function and exercise performance in humans. In addition, research that has investigated the potential synergistic effects of L-citrulline with other dietary ingredients (e.g., arginine, antioxidants, nitrates, and branched-chain amino acids) is reviewed. Oral L-citrulline and citrulline malate supplementation have shown to increase plasma citrulline and arginine concentrations, along with total nitrate and nitrite concentrations. Although blood flow enhancement is a proposed mechanism for the ergogenic potential of L-citrulline, evidence supporting acute improvements in vasodilation and skeletal muscle tissue perfusion after supplementation is scarce and inconsistent. Nevertheless, several studies have reported that L-citrulline supplementation can enhance exercise performance and recovery. Given the positive effects observed from some investigations, future studies should continue to investigate the effects of both acute and chronic supplementation with L-citrulline and citrulline malate on markers of blood flow and exercise performance and should seek to elucidate the mechanism underlying such effects.

studies.title: Short-term citrulline malate supplementation enhances lower-limb function in physically active older women: A pilot randomized controlled trial.
studies.abstract: This pilot randomized controlled trial examined whether short-term (6-week) citrulline malate (CM) supplementation combined with multicomponent exercise could improve physical function, metabolic biomarkers, and quality of life in physically active older women. Twenty community-dwelling women aged 60-75 years were randomized to a 6-week exercise program (3 sessions/week) plus 3 g/day CM (n = 10) or placebo (n = 10). Outcomes were assessed pre- and post-intervention and included physical performance (sit-to-stand test, 6-min walk test [6MWT], Short Physical Performance Battery [SPPB]), blood biomarkers (25-hydroxyvitamin D [25(OH)D], cortisol, testosterone, creatine kinase, glucose), and quality of life (WHOQOL-BREF). The CM group showed significant improvement in sit-to-stand performance (Δ = -1.62 ± 1.49 s; p = 0.023; d = 1.38). Trends towards greater improvements were observed in 6MWT distance (+61.0 ± 80.2 m vs. +15.8 ± 28.9 m; d = 0.65) and SPPB score (+0.60 ± 0.55 vs. -0.09 ± 0.70; d = 1.05) compared with placebo, although between-group differences were not statistically significant. Serum 25(OH)D increased with CM (+3.82 ± 5.01 ng/mL) and decreased with placebo (-0.90 ± 4.71 ng/mL). No significant between-group differences were observed in other biomarkers or quality-of-life domains. No adverse events were reported during the intervention. Six weeks of CM supplementation combined with multicomponent training was associated with improved sit-to-stand performance in older women, with additional favourable trends in walking endurance, SPPB score, and 25(OH)D. Given the pilot nature of the study, these findings should be considered preliminary and hypothesis-generating. Larger and longer trials are needed to confirm the reproducibility, clinical significance, and potential mechanisms of these effects.

studies.title: Acute citrulline-malate supplementation is ineffective during aerobic cycling and subsequent anaerobic performance in recreationally active males.
studies.abstract: Citrulline-malate (CM) purportedly increases exercise performance through increased nitric oxide production. The effects of CM on muscular strength performance are well-documented; however, the benefits of CM on aerobic and anaerobic biking performance are not well researched. Therefore, the present investigation examined the acute CM supplementation effects on aerobic and anaerobic cycling performance in recreationally active males.

studies.title: Inter-Individual Responses to Citrulline Malate Oral Supplementation on Post-Exercise Hypotension in Hypertensives: A 24-Hour Analysis.
studies.abstract: Studies have persuasively demonstrated that citrulline has a key role in the arginine-nitric oxide system, increasing nitric oxide bioavailability, an important mediator of peripheral vasodilation. To analyze the inter-individual post-exercise hypotension responsiveness following acute citrulline supplementation in hypertensives. Forty hypertensives were randomly assigned to one of the four experimental groups (control-placebo, control-citrulline, exercise-placebo, and exercise-citrulline). They ingested placebo or citrulline malate [CM] (6 grams). During the exercise session, individuals performed 40 minutes of walking/running on a treadmill at 60-70% of HR reserve. For the control session, the individuals remained seated at rest for 40 minutes. Office blood pressure (BP) was taken every 10 minutes until completing 60 minutes after the experimental session. The ambulatory BP device was programmed to take the readings every 20 minutes (awake time) and every 30 minutes (sleep time) over the course of 24 hours of monitoring. Statistical significance was defined as p < 0.05. Unlike the other experimental groups, there were no "non-responders" in the exercise/citrulline (EC) for "awake" (systolic and diastolic BP) and "24 hours" (diastolic BP). The effect sizes were more consistent in the EC for systolic and diastolic ambulatorial BP response. The effects were "large" (> 0.8) for "awake", "asleep", and "24 hours" only in the EC for diastolic BP. CM supplementation can increase the post-exercise hypotensive effects in hypertensives. In addition, the prevalence of non-responders is lower when associated with aerobic exercise and CM supplementation.

studies.title: Acute citrulline malate supplementation improves upper- and lower-body submaximal weightlifting exercise performance in resistance-trained females.
studies.abstract: Citrulline malate (CM) is a nonessential amino acid that increases exercise performance in males. However, based on physiological differences between genders, these results cannot be extrapolated to females. Therefore, the purpose of this investigation was to evaluate effects of acute CM supplementation on upper- and lower-body weightlifting performance in resistance-trained females. Fifteen females (23 ± 3 years) completed two randomized, double-blind trials consuming either CM (8 g dextrose + 8 g CM) or a placebo (8 g dextrose). One hour after supplement consumption, participants performed six sets each of upper- (i.e., bench press) and lower-body (i.e., leg press) exercises to failure at 80 % of previously established one-repetition maximum. Immediately after each set, repetitions completed, heart rate and rating of perceived exertion (RPE) were recorded. Repeated-measures analysis of variance indicated that subjects completed significantly (p = .045) more repetitions throughout upper-body exercise when consuming CM versus placebo (34.1 ± 5.7 vs. 32.9 ± 6.0, respectively). When consuming CM, similar significant (p = .03) improvements in total repetitions completed were observed for lower-body exercise (66.7 ± 30.5 vs. 55.13 ± 20.64, respectively). Overall RPE score was significantly lower (p = .02) in upper-body exercise when subjects consumed CM versus placebo (7.9 ± 0.3 and 8.6 ± 0.2, respectively). The supplement consumed exhibited no significant effects on heart rate at any time point. Acute CM supplementation in females increased upper- and lower-body resistance exercise performance and decreased RPE during upper-body exercise. These data indicate that athletes competing in sports with muscular endurance-based requirements may potentially improve performance by acutely supplementing CM.

Results

Metabolic variables measured twice before CM ingestion showed no differences, indicating good reproducibility of measurements and no learning effect from repeating the exercise protocol. CM ingestion resulted in a significant reduction in the sensation of fatigue, a 34% increase in the rate of oxidative ATP production during exercise, and a 20% increase in the rate of phosphocreatine recovery after exercise, indicating a larger contribution of oxidative ATP synthesis to energy production. Considering subjects individually and variables characterising aerobic function, extrema were measured after either eight or 15 days of treatment, indicating chronological heterogeneity of treatment induced changes. One way analysis of variance confirmed improved aerobic function, which may be the result of an enhanced malate supply activating ATP production from the tricarboxylic acid cycle through anaplerotic reactions.

Conclusion

The changes in muscle metabolism produced by CM treatment indicate that CM may promote aerobic energy production.

studies.title: Overview of mechanisms related to citrulline malate supplementation and different methods of high-intensity interval training on sports performance: A narrative
studies.abstract: Regular exercise is a practical non-pharmacological approach to maintaining physical and mental health through rehabilitation and prevention of chronic diseases due to its cardiovascular, cardiorespiratory, neurological, and neuromuscular benefits. Despite awareness of the benefits of exercise, a “lack of time” has proven to be the most common impediment to regular activity. Thus, a time-efficient and potentially enjoyable training modality with growing popularity is high-intensity interval training (HIIT). HIIT incorporates intermittent bouts of work and recovery intervals performed at an intensity close to maximal oxygen consumption (VO₂max). HIIT is considered to have equivalent or superior benefits compared to moderate-intensity continuous training (MICT). This narrative review focuses on the mechanisms of Citrulline Malate (CM) supplementation and various modes of HIIT on exercise performance. CM serves as a nitric-oxide enhancer leading to improved aerobic and anaerobic exercise performance by increasing muscle adenosine triphosphate (ATP) production, vasodilation, and blood flow to the active musculature and boosting work capacity. This article reviews the mechanisms related to CM supplementation and different modes of HIIT on exercise performance. Even though a single, acute 8 g dose of CM has been recommended, its mechanism of action remains to be seen due to the synergistic impact of both components (citrulline and malate). Moreover, the limited evidence for the standard level of supplement use and source of purchase results in athletes’ self-prescription of supplements. Therefore, to reduce the risk of accidental doping or toxicity, further studies should continue to investigate the optimal dose, timing, mechanism of action, as well as reliable sources of purchase for CM consumption.

explanation.what_it_is_line: An amino acid compound that helps cells produce nitric oxide, a signaling molecule that relaxes blood vessels.
explanation.what_it_is: Citrulline malate is a combination of L-citrulline (an amino acid — one of the building blocks your cells use to make proteins and other molecules) bonded to malate (an organic acid). It's naturally present in small amounts in foods like watermelon, but supplements contain much larger doses. People typically take it as a powder or capsule, usually 30 minutes to an hour before exercise.
explanation.how_it_works_line: Boosts nitric oxide to widen blood vessels and improve blood flow, helping muscles get more oxygen and nutrients.
explanation.how_it_works: When you swallow citrulline malate, your body converts the citrulline into nitric oxide — a chemical messenger that tells blood vessel walls to relax and widen. Wider vessels allow more blood to flow to your muscles during and after exercise, delivering oxygen and nutrients more efficiently. Nitric oxide also helps reduce the buildup of lactate (a byproduct of intense muscle work) and may lower the amount of effort your nervous system perceives during hard exercise. Better blood flow and lower perceived fatigue are the reasons it's studied for athletic performance and recovery.
explanation.safety_line: Well-tolerated in short-term use; long-term safety and effects in specific populations remain untested.
explanation.safety_detail: Published trials report few serious side effects from short-term citrulline malate supplementation in healthy, mostly young and middle-aged adults. Mild gastrointestinal symptoms (nausea, bloating) have been noted in some studies. However, trials are typically brief (days to weeks), enroll narrow populations (mostly trained or recreationally active people), and do not formally assess long-term safety.
safety_bullets: Long-term safety (months to years of continuous use) has not been systematically studied in retrieved trials.
Pregnant women, nursing mothers, and adolescents under 18 were excluded from or absent in the studies provided — effects in these groups are unknown.
Potential interactions with nitrate-containing medications or other arginine-metabolism agents have not been evaluated in the retrieved records.
People with severe kidney or liver disease were not enrolled in trials provided — safety in these populations is untested.
explanation.chem_meaning: Citrulline malate is a relatively large, polar (water-attracting) molecule, which means it dissolves well in water and is absorbed through the intestine but does not easily cross the blood–brain barrier. The malate component adds additional metabolic activity — it participates in the cell's energy-production cycle (the citric acid cycle) — which may enhance the supplement's effect beyond citrulline alone, though this is still being investigated.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2022 meta-analysis and several systematic reviews (2020–2026) examined exercise performance in resistance-trained and recreationally active adults. Pooled data across 25 human studies showed a small average benefit (hedges g 0.196), meaning people performed modestly more repetitions or work output after taking citrulline malate versus placebo. A 2021 meta-analysis of 137 participants specifically on repetition performance during strength training and a 2020 analysis of 206 participants on perceived exertion and muscle soreness both found modest improvements. Results were consistent in direction but varied in magnitude, and most individual trial sample sizes were small (n=10–20).
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Multiple meta-analyses and systematic reviews confirm a small benefit across diverse exercise settings, but individual studies are small and heterogeneous in methods and outcomes, limiting certainty about the true effect size and who benefits most.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2022 meta-analysis and 2021 meta-analysis (n=137) on repetition performance during strength training, along with several RCTs from 2021–2025, examined resistance-trained and recreationally active adults. A 2023 RCT found acute citrulline-malate supplementation increased total work in short lower-body isokinetic tasks. A 2025 RCT examined changes in resistance training performance and blood biomarkers after six weeks. Collectively, 17 human studies showed modest improvements in strength-related outcomes, though one 2021 RCT found it ineffective during aerobic cycling. Verified sample sizes range from ~10 to 137 per study.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Consistent direction of benefit across multiple meta-analyses and RCTs, but individual trial sizes are small and results vary, suggesting a genuine but modest effect that does not meet the threshold for Strong evidence.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2020 meta-analysis of 206 participants specifically examined post-exercise muscle soreness and rating of perceived exertion, finding modest reductions. Additional meta-analyses (2021–2022) and RCTs (2020–2026) evaluated soreness and recovery markers across resistance training and sprint tasks. A 2026 RCT tested acute effects on 100 m sprint performance in trained sprinters. Studies consistently showed small to modest improvements in perceived soreness and fatigue, and several reported faster lactate clearance (the body's ability to remove a fatigue byproduct). Twenty human studies were retrieved; verified sample sizes range from ~10 to 206.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Multiple meta-analyses and systematic reviews support a small benefit on perceived soreness and exertion across diverse exercise modes, but heterogeneity in study designs and outcome measures, plus small individual trial sizes, prevent a stronger grade.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Eight human studies examined endurance capacity — including a 2021 meta-analysis on repetition performance, a 2026 RCT in older women (n=10), a 2025 RCT on resistance training performance and biomarkers, a 2021 RCT on aerobic cycling (which found citrulline-malate ineffective), and a 2019 RCT on post-exercise blood pressure in hypertensive adults. The evidence is mixed: some studies support modest improvements in lower-limb endurance and work capacity, while at least one found no effect on aerobic cycling. Verified sample sizes are small (n=10–137 where reported).
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Limited number of primary endurance studies (5 standalone trials plus 2 pooled analyses) and inconsistent findings between aerobic and resistance endurance tasks, combined with small and heterogeneous populations, place this below the threshold for Strong evidence.

explanation.evidence_base: The evidence base comprises 25–20 human studies, mostly RCTs and meta-analyses published between 2019 and 2026, with a small number of animal studies also retrieved. Most trials are relatively short-term (acute dosing or 6 weeks), enroll trained or recreationally active adults, and measure strength, power, or soreness via standardized protocols. Verified sample sizes in published abstracts range from ~10 to 206, though the true total across all retrieved studies is larger. No large, long-term trials in diverse populations (e.g., older adults, clinical populations) were identified in the records provided.
explanation.open_questions: The provided records show that citrulline malate has been tested primarily in young to middle-aged, trained or recreationally active people; older adults, sedentary individuals, and people with chronic disease are nearly absent from the sample. All outcomes rely on short-term supplementation (days to weeks); no study in the records examined chronic use over months or years. Effects in specific exercise modalities are inconsistent — aerobic cycling, for instance, showed no benefit in one trial — suggesting that the benefit may be context-dependent, but the records do not fully clarify when and in whom it works best.

appraisal.headline: Most studies omit sample sizes and no pooled meta-analyses confirm agreement across trials, making it impossible to verify whether the small observed effects (g=0.196 for exercise performance) are real or driven by selective reporting and publication bias.

concerns.issue: Severe reporting opacity on sample sizes
concerns.detail: Across all four outcomes, only 2–4 of 19–27 studies per outcome report sample size in the abstracts. The exercise performance outcome cites only 4 of 27 studies with n reported; muscle soreness reports 2 of 24. The engine estimates 'true total substantially larger,' but without access to full papers, the actual precision and generalizability remain completely opaque. A pooled n could range from ~300 to >2000 participants depending on unreported trial sizes.

concerns.issue: No confirmed meta-analytic synthesis despite multiple reviews
concerns.detail: Three meta-analyses and five systematic reviews are listed for exercise performance alone, yet the engine explicitly notes 'no pooled analysis confirms they agree' and holds inconsistency at 'moderate pending review.' This suggests the reviews may differ substantially in scope, eligibility criteria, or extracted data—yet no abstract discloses pooled effect sizes or heterogeneity statistics. The pooled effect of g=0.196 appears to derive from a single secondary calculation, not from any published consensus analysis.

concerns.issue: Weak and uncertain pooled effect with CI crossing zero
concerns.detail: For exercise performance, the only extractable pooled effect is g=0.196 [0.0 to 0.392]—the 95% CI includes zero, indicating the lower bound of the evidence is null effect. Expressed as a practical threshold, this is a 2–5% improvement in repetitions or time, well within day-to-day noise and placebo-responsive outcomes. No other outcome (muscle strength, soreness, endurance) reports an extractable pooled effect at all.

concerns.issue: Extreme recency and design heterogeneity in primary studies
concerns.detail: Seven of the ten most recent trials listed are from 2025–2026, and the design mix includes RCTs, unclassified studies, and animal trials without clear stratification. One trial enrolled only 10 participants (2026 RCT on older adults), another 13 (2024 sprint study). The median reported n is 137 (from meta-analyses, not primaries), but median primary trial size appears much smaller. This clustering at recent publication dates raises concerns about selective emergence of positive findings and regression to the mean in newer, smaller trials.

concerns.issue: Outcome-specific evidence is sparse and heterogeneous
concerns.detail: Endurance has only 5 primary human RCTs and 1 meta-analysis; one 2021 trial explicitly reports citrulline-malate was 'ineffective during aerobic cycling.' Muscle soreness and strength outcomes show no extractable pooled effects at all, despite 11–13 RCTs each, implying high inconsistency or incompatible outcome reporting. The evidence base conflates acute dosing (single dose before exercise) with chronic supplementation protocols, making it unclear whether effects generalize.

appraisal.mechanism_check: Citrulline increases nitric oxide bioavailability, which plausibly improves blood flow and reduces fatigue—this chain is biologically sound. However, the leap from improved NO signaling to measurable gains in repetitions, soreness, or endurance requires that the effect size be large enough to overcome inter-individual variability and detection noise; the observed g=0.196 is below the typical minimal clinically important difference for strength or performance outcomes. The mechanism does not guarantee the magnitude of clinical effect observed.
appraisal.strongest_counterargument: A skeptic would note that (1) the single pooled effect for exercise performance (g=0.196, CI 0.0–0.392) is barely distinguishable from zero and likely represents placebo or reporting bias rather than true pharmacology, (2) multiple reviews exist but report conflicting conclusions without published synthesis, suggesting the literature is fragmented and inconclusive, and (3) recent trials are small (n=10–13) and highly responsive to both placebo and baseline imbalance. The 2021 trial showing ineffectiveness during aerobic cycling suggests the compound does not work uniformly, contradicting a general 'performance enhancer' claim.
appraisal.what_would_change_the_picture: A large, multi-center RCT (n≥150) with pre-registered primary outcomes, standardized dosing (acute vs. chronic clearly separated), and outcome assessment blinded to allocation, published in full with sample size justification and heterogeneity analysis, comparing citrulline-malate to active control (not placebo) in a single, well-defined population (e.g., trained resistance athletes) would resolve whether the effect is real and generalizable. Publication of a Cochrane-grade systematic review with meta-regression on dose, timing, and population would also clarify the conflicting signals in the current literature.

explanation_es.what_it_is_line: Un compuesto de aminoácido que ayuda a las células a producir óxido nítrico, una molécula de señalización que relaja los vasos sanguíneos.
explanation_es.what_it_is: El malato de citrulina es una combinación de L-citrulina (un aminoácido — uno de los bloques de construcción que tus células usan para hacer proteínas y otras moléculas) unido al malato (un ácido orgánico). Está presente naturalmente en pequeñas cantidades en alimentos como la sandía, pero los suplementos contienen dosis mucho más grandes. Las personas típicamente lo toman en forma de polvo o cápsula, generalmente 30 minutos a una hora antes del ejercicio.
explanation_es.how_it_works_line: Aumenta el óxido nítrico para dilatar los vasos sanguíneos y mejorar el flujo de sangre, ayudando a los músculos a obtener más oxígeno y nutrientes.
explanation_es.how_it_works: Cuando tragas malato de citrulina, tu cuerpo convierte la citrulina en óxido nítrico — un mensajero químico que le dice a las paredes de los vasos sanguíneos que se relajen y se dilaten. Los vasos más anchos permiten que más sangre fluya hacia tus músculos durante y después del ejercicio, entregando oxígeno y nutrientes de manera más eficiente. El óxido nítrico también ayuda a reducir la acumulación de lactato (un subproducto del trabajo muscular intenso) y puede disminuir la cantidad de esfuerzo que tu sistema nervioso percibe durante ejercicio intenso. El mejor flujo de sangre y la fatiga percibida reducida son las razones por las que se estudia para el rendimiento atlético y la recuperación.
explanation_es.safety_line: Bien tolerado en uso a corto plazo; la seguridad a largo plazo y los efectos en poblaciones específicas permanecen sin evaluar.
explanation_es.safety_detail: Los ensayos publicados reportan pocos efectos secundarios graves del suplemento de malato de citrulina a corto plazo en adultos sanos, mayormente jóvenes y de edad mediana. Se han observado síntomas gastrointestinales leves (náuseas, hinchazón) en algunos estudios. Sin embargo, los ensayos son típicamente breves (días a semanas), reclutan poblaciones estrechas (mayormente personas entrenadas o activas recreativamente), y no evalúan formalmente la seguridad a largo plazo.
safety_bullets: La seguridad a largo plazo (meses a años de uso continuo) no ha sido estudiada sistemáticamente en los ensayos recuperados.
Las mujeres embarazadas, las madres lactantes y los adolescentes menores de 18 años fueron excluidos o ausentes en los estudios proporcionados — los efectos en estos grupos son desconocidos.
Las posibles interacciones con medicamentos que contienen nitratos u otros agentes del metabolismo de la arginina no han sido evaluadas en los registros recuperados.
Las personas con enfermedad renal o hepática severa no fueron inscritas en los ensayos proporcionados — la seguridad en estas poblaciones no ha sido probada.
explanation_es.chem_meaning: El malato de citrulina es una molécula relativamente grande y polar (que atrae agua), lo que significa que se disuelve bien en agua y se absorbe a través del intestino pero no cruza fácilmente la barrera hematoencefálica. El componente malato añade actividad metabólica adicional — participa en el ciclo de producción de energía de la célula (el ciclo del ácido cítrico) — lo que puede mejorar el efecto del suplemento más allá de la citrulina sola, aunque esto aún está siendo investigado.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Un metanálisis de 2022 y varios análisis sistemáticos (2020–2026) examinaron el rendimiento del ejercicio en adultos entrenados en resistencia y activos recreativamente. Los datos agrupados de 25 estudios humanos mostraron un beneficio promedio pequeño (hedges g 0.196), lo que significa que las personas realizaron modestamente más repeticiones o volumen de trabajo después de tomar malato de citrulina versus placebo. Un metanálisis de 2021 de 137 participantes específicamente sobre rendimiento de repeticiones durante entrenamiento de fuerza y un análisis de 2020 de 206 participantes sobre percepción de esfuerzo y dolor muscular ambos encontraron mejoras modestas. Los resultados fueron consistentes en dirección pero variaron en magnitud, y la mayoría de los tamaños de muestra individuales fueron pequeños (n=10–20).
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Múltiples metanálisis y análisis sistemáticos confirman un beneficio pequeño en diversos escenarios de ejercicio, pero los estudios individuales son pequeños y heterogéneos en métodos y resultados, limitando la certeza sobre el verdadero tamaño del efecto y quién se beneficia más.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Un metanálisis de 2022 y un metanálisis de 2021 (n=137) sobre rendimiento de repeticiones durante entrenamiento de fuerza, junto con varios ECA de 2021–2025, examinaron adultos entrenados en resistencia y activos recreativamente. Un ECA de 2023 encontró que la suplementación aguda de malato de citrulina aumentó el trabajo total en tareas isocinéticas cortas de miembros inferiores. Un ECA de 2025 examinó cambios en el rendimiento del entrenamiento de resistencia y biomarcadores sanguíneos después de seis semanas. En conjunto, 17 estudios humanos mostraron mejoras modestas en resultados relacionados con la fuerza, aunque un ECA de 2021 encontró que era inefectivo durante ciclismo aeróbico. Los tamaños de muestra verificados oscilan entre aproximadamente 10 y 137 por estudio.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: La dirección consistente del beneficio en múltiples metanálisis y ECA, pero los tamaños de ensayo individuales son pequeños y los resultados varían, sugiriendo un efecto genuino pero modesto que no alcanza el umbral para evidencia Fuerte.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Un metanálisis de 2020 de 206 participantes examinó específicamente el dolor muscular post-ejercicio y la puntuación de esfuerzo percibido, encontrando reducciones modestas. Los metanálisis adicionales (2021–2022) y ECA (2020–2026) evaluaron el dolor muscular y los marcadores de recuperación en entrenamiento de resistencia y tareas de sprint. Un ECA de 2026 probó efectos agudos en el rendimiento de sprint de 100 m en corredores de sprint entrenados. Los estudios mostraron consistentemente mejoras pequeñas a modestas en el dolor percibido y la fatiga, y varios reportaron aclaramiento más rápido de lactato (la capacidad del cuerpo de eliminar un subproducto de la fatiga). Se recuperaron 20 estudios humanos; los tamaños de muestra verificados oscilan entre aproximadamente 10 y 206.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Múltiples metanálisis y análisis sistemáticos apoyan un beneficio pequeño en el dolor percibido y el esfuerzo en diversos modos de ejercicio, pero la heterogeneidad en los diseños de estudio y las medidas de resultado, más los tamaños pequeños de ensayo individual, impiden una calificación más fuerte.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Ocho estudios humanos examinaron la capacidad de resistencia — incluyendo un metanálisis de 2021 sobre rendimiento de repeticiones, un ECA de 2026 en mujeres mayores (n=10), un ECA de 2025 sobre rendimiento de entrenamiento de resistencia y biomarcadores, un ECA de 2021 sobre ciclismo aeróbico (que encontró malato de citrulina inefectivo), y un ECA de 2019 sobre presión arterial post-ejercicio en adultos hipertensos. La evidencia es mixta: algunos estudios apoyan mejoras modestas en la resistencia de miembros inferiores y la capacidad de trabajo, mientras que al menos uno no encontró efecto en ciclismo aeróbico. Los tamaños de muestra verificados son pequeños (n=10–137 donde se reportaron).
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Número limitado de estudios primarios de resistencia (5 ensayos independientes más 2 análisis agrupados) y hallazgos inconsistentes entre tareas de resistencia aeróbica y de resistencia, combinado con poblaciones pequeñas y heterogéneas, colocan esto por debajo del umbral para evidencia Fuerte.

explanation_es.evidence_base: La base de evidencia comprende 25–20 estudios humanos, mayormente ECA y metanálisis publicados entre 2019 y 2026, con un número pequeño de estudios en animales también recuperados. La mayoría de los ensayos son relativamente a corto plazo (dosificación aguda o 6 semanas), reclutan adultos entrenados o activos recreativamente, y miden fuerza, potencia o dolor a través de protocolos estandarizados. Los tamaños de muestra verificados en los resúmenes publicados oscilan entre aproximadamente 10 y 206, aunque el verdadero total de todos los estudios recuperados es más grande. No se identificaron ensayos grandes y a largo plazo en poblaciones diversas (p. ej., adultos mayores, poblaciones clínicas) en los registros proporcionados.
explanation_es.open_questions: Los registros proporcionados muestran que el malato de citrulina ha sido probado principalmente en personas jóvenes a edad mediana, entrenadas o activas recreativamente; los adultos mayores, las personas sedentarias y las personas con enfermedades crónicas están casi ausentes de la muestra. Todos los resultados se basan en suplementación a corto plazo (días a semanas); ningún estudio en los registros examinó el uso crónico durante meses o años. Los efectos en modalidades de ejercicio específicas son inconsistentes — el ciclismo aeróbico, por ejemplo, no mostró beneficio en un ensayo — sugiriendo que el beneficio puede ser dependiente del contexto, pero los registros no aclaran completamente cuándo y en quién funciona mejor.

appraisal_es.headline: La mayoría de los estudios omiten tamaños de muestra y ningún metanálisis agrupado confirma acuerdo entre ensayos, lo que hace imposible verificar si los pequeños efectos observados (g=0.196 para rendimiento en ejercicio) son reales o están impulsados por sesgo de reporte selectivo y sesgo de publicación.

concerns.issue: Opacidad severa en la notificación de tamaños de muestra
concerns.detail: En los cuatro resultados, solo 2–4 de 19–27 estudios por resultado informan el tamaño de muestra en los resúmenes. El resultado de rendimiento en ejercicio cita solo 4 de 27 estudios con n reportado; el dolor muscular informa 2 de 24. El motor estima que 'el verdadero total probablemente sea sustancialmente mayor,' pero sin acceso a los artículos completos, la precisión y generalización real permanecen completamente opacos. Una n agrupada podría oscilar de ~300 a >2000 participantes dependiendo de los tamaños de ensayo no reportados.

concerns.issue: Sin síntesis metaanalítica confirmada a pesar de múltiples revisiones
concerns.detail: Se enumeran tres metanálisis y cinco revisiones sistemáticas solo para rendimiento en ejercicio, sin embargo, el motor explícitamente señala 'ningún análisis agrupado confirma que estén de acuerdo' y mantiene la inconsistencia en 'moderada pendiente de revisión.' Esto sugiere que las revisiones pueden diferir sustancialmente en alcance, criterios de elegibilidad o datos extraídos—sin embargo, ningún resumen divulga tamaños de efectos agrupados o estadísticas de heterogeneidad. El efecto agrupado de g=0.196 parece derivar de un único cálculo secundario, no de ningún análisis de consenso publicado.

concerns.issue: Efecto agrupado débil e incierto con IC cruzando cero
concerns.detail: Para rendimiento en ejercicio, el único efecto agrupado extraíble es g=0.196 [0.0 a 0.392]—el IC del 95% incluye cero, indicando que el límite inferior de la evidencia es efecto nulo. Expresado como un umbral práctico, esto es una mejora del 2–5% en repeticiones o tiempo, bien dentro del ruido día a día y resultados responsivos al placebo. Ningún otro resultado (fuerza muscular, dolor, resistencia) reporta un efecto agrupado extraíble en absoluto.

concerns.issue: Recencia extrema y heterogeneidad de diseño en estudios primarios
concerns.detail: Siete de los diez ensayos más recientes listados son de 2025–2026, y la mezcla de diseños incluye ECA, estudios no clasificados y ensayos en animales sin estratificación clara. Un ensayo enroló solo 10 participantes (ECA 2026 en adultos mayores), otro 13 (estudio de sprint 2024). La n mediana reportada es 137 (de metanálisis, no primarios), pero el tamaño de ensayo primario mediano parece mucho más pequeño. Este agrupamiento en fechas de publicación recientes genera preocupación sobre la emergencia selectiva de hallazgos positivos y regresión a la media en ensayos más nuevos y pequeños.

concerns.issue: La evidencia específica por resultado es escasa y heterogénea
concerns.detail: La resistencia tiene solo 5 ECA humanos primarios y 1 metanálisis; un ensayo 2021 explícitamente reporta que citrulina-malato fue 'inefectiva durante ciclismo aeróbico.' Los resultados de dolor muscular y fuerza muestran ningún efecto agrupado extraíble en absoluto, a pesar de 11–13 ECA cada uno, lo que implica alta inconsistencia o reporte de resultados incompatible. La base de evidencia conflúe dosificación aguda (dosis única antes del ejercicio) con protocolos de suplementación crónica, lo que hace incierto si los efectos se generalizan.

appraisal_es.mechanism_check: La citrulina aumenta la biodisponibilidad del óxido nítrico, lo que plausiblemente mejora el flujo sanguíneo y reduce la fatiga—esta cadena es biológicamente sólida. Sin embargo, el salto de la señalización de NO mejorada a ganancias medibles en repeticiones, dolor o resistencia requiere que el tamaño del efecto sea lo suficientemente grande para superar la variabilidad interindividual y el ruido de detección; la g=0.196 observada está por debajo de la diferencia clinicamente importante mínima típica para resultados de fuerza o rendimiento. El mecanismo no garantiza la magnitud del efecto clínico observado.
appraisal_es.strongest_counterargument: Un escéptico notaría que (1) el único efecto agrupado para rendimiento en ejercicio (g=0.196, IC 0.0–0.392) es apenas distinguible de cero e probablemente representa sesgo de placebo o reporte en lugar de farmacología verdadera, (2) múltiples revisiones existen pero reportan conclusiones conflictivas sin síntesis publicada, sugiriendo que la literatura es fragmentada e inconclusa, y (3) ensayos recientes son pequeños (n=10–13) y altamente responsivos tanto al placebo como al desequilibrio basal. El ensayo 2021 mostrando inefectividad durante ciclismo aeróbico sugiere que el compuesto no funciona uniformemente, contradiciendo un reclamo general de 'potenciador de rendimiento.'
appraisal_es.what_would_change_the_picture: Un ECA grande, multicéntrico (n≥150) con resultados primarios pre-registrados, dosificación estandarizada (aguda vs. crónica claramente separadas) y evaluación de resultados cegada para asignación, publicado en su totalidad con justificación del tamaño de muestra y análisis de heterogeneidad, comparando citrulina-malato con control activo (no placebo) en una única población bien definida (p. ej., atletas de resistencia entrenados) resolvería si el efecto es real y generalizable. La publicación de una revisión sistemática de calidad Cochrane con metarregresión en dosis, temporización y población también aclararía las señales conflictivas en la literatura actual.
